newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen's ruling party boycotts parliament session.
newsitem.headline: Yemen's ruling party boycotts parliament session.

text.p: Yemen's ruling political party boycotted a parliamentary session on Sunday in protest against the assembly speaker's call for a debate on recent price rises, a leading party official said.
President Ali Abdullah Saleh's General People's Congress (GPC) dominates the assembly, holding 187 of the 301 seats.

"The GPC parliamentary bloc did not attend today's (Sunday's) parliamentary session in protest against a decision to summon the government for a general discussion on recent price increases," the official said.

He said the GPC bloc walked out on Saturday and boycotted Sunday's session after speaker Sheikh Abdullah bin Hussein al-Ahmar called for the debate, a move the GPC said violated parliamentary regulations.

"The head of the bloc, Sultan al-Bakarani, tried to explain to the parliamentary speaker that according to parliamentary regulations, 60 percent of deputies attending the session should agree on the decision to request the government for such a debate," he said.
Parliamentary sources said the boycott disrupted the 101 quorum required for the session to proceed.
"The speaker responded in an inappropriate way to Bakarani, a matter which made the GPC angry and made it withdraw," the official said, but did not elaborate.
Ahmar is a member of the opposition Islah party, which won only 53 seats in April's general elections. GPC and Islah ruled in coalition before the poll.

In early July Yemen raised wheat and flour prices by around 14 percent in line with recommendations by the International Monetary Fund, only a few hours after the oil ministry raised petrol prices by more than 31 percent.

When Yemen, one of the region's poorest countries, last raised the price of petrol in 1996, farmers and students took to the streets in protest. In 1995, riots erupted in the southern port city of Aden over the doubling of petrol prices.
Islah has voiced concern about economic reforms demanded by the IMF and World Bank, saying they entailed high social costs.
The GPC official said the party was still holding talks on how to proceed, and had not yet decided about returning to take up their seats in parliament.
